lines.text: Most people assume a USB-C charging cable is just a passive bundle of copper wires inside plastic.
In reality, high-power USB-C cables contain an active computer inside the plug: an electronic marker chip.
Standard copper wires can safely carry three amps of current. Forcing five amps through thin wire produces violent resistive heating and melts the insulation.
To prevent electrical fires, the E-Marker chip negotiates directly with your charger using high-frequency packets on the Configuration Channel pin.
It broadcasts its vendor identity, wire gauge rating, and maximum voltage: authorizing up to two hundred and forty watts under Extended Power Range.
If your charger doesn't detect that digital signature, it hard-caps electrical current to sixty watts, protecting cheap cables from burning.
USB-C didn't just unify our connectors: it turned dumb copper wire into a communicating computer on your desk.
